zh.q: 这块土壤标本自上而下能分出几层？
zh.concl: 土壤剖面是从地面垂直向下的纵剖面，由形态特征各异、大致水平展布的土层构成；自然土壤中森林土壤剖面最复杂，自上而下是有机层、腐殖质层、淋溶层、淀积层、母质层、母岩层。
points: 土壤由矿物质、有机质、水分和空气四种物质组成；野外观察看颜色、质地、剖面构造（教材 p.88）。
剖面是从地面垂直向下的纵剖面，土层大致呈水平展布，是物质转化、迁移、积累的结果。
森林土壤剖面最复杂，六层自上而下：有机层 → 腐殖质层 → 淋溶层 → 淀积层 → 母质层 → 母岩层；有机质越往下越少。

zh.q: 母质不同，土壤的质地会怎样变？
zh.concl: 成土母质是岩石的风化产物，是土壤发育的物质基础；它决定土壤矿物质的成分和养分状况，影响土壤的质地。
points: 成土母质是岩石的风化产物，是土壤发育的物质基础。
它决定土壤矿物质的成分和养分状况，影响土壤的质地：砂质母质 → 砾质土 / 砂土，黏质母质 → 黏土。
四川盆地的岩石是紫色的，土壤也呈紫色——这条现象的主导因素就是成土母质。

zh.q: 把植被去掉，这块土还会是土壤吗？
zh.concl: 生物是影响土壤发育最基本也是最活跃的因素；生物残体提供有机质、微生物把有机质变成腐殖质，生物循环使营养元素在土壤表层富集。
points: 生物是影响土壤发育最基本也是最活跃的因素——没有生物的作用，就不可能形成土壤。
生物残体为土壤提供有机质，有机质在微生物作用下转化为腐殖质。
生物循环把氮、磷、钾等营养元素搬到土壤表层富集：生物 0 % 时有机层与腐殖质层都消失、有机质为 0。

zh.q: 同样的母质，湿热和干冷会养出一样的土吗？
zh.concl: 水热条件决定风化和淋溶的快慢：湿热地区成土快、黏粒多、淋溶强、有机质分解快；冷湿环境有利于有机质积累，干旱高温地区积累少。
points: 岩石风化的强度和速度与温度、降水量呈正相关，所以湿热地区的土壤形成速度比干冷地区快得多。
湿热地区化学风化与淋溶作用强，土壤黏粒比重高；冷湿环境有利于有机质积累，干旱、高温地区有机质积累少。
注意：雨量和气温只改黏粒占比，不改质地名称——质地由母质与地貌定。

zh.q: 山顶和山前平原的土，颗粒一样粗吗？
zh.concl: 从山顶到低平洼地，成土母质的颗粒由粗到细，依次分布着砾质土、砂土、壤土和黏土；所以山顶的土颗粒较粗、山前平原较细。
points: 地貌通过水热条件与母质颗粒的分选影响土壤发育。
从山顶到低平洼地，成土母质的颗粒存在由粗到细的变化规律：砾质土 → 砂土 → 壤土 → 黏土。
壤土的砂粒、粉粒、黏粒比例适中，通气透水又蓄水保肥，是农业生产理想的土壤质地。

zh.q: 挖下去 20 cm 的土，要多久才能长出来？
zh.concl: 土壤发育的时间越长，土壤层越厚、土层分化越明显；自然状态下形成 20 cm 厚可供耕作的土壤一般需要 100—1 000 年。
points: 土壤发育的时间越长，土壤层越厚，土层分化越明显。
在自然状态下，形成 20 cm 厚可供耕作的土壤，一般需要 100—1 000 年。
所以柱子里的每一厘米土层都是「攒」出来的：母岩层被风化掉一层，土层就厚一层。

zh.q: 一块地被长期耕种，剖面会变成什么样？
zh.concl: 自然土壤经长期耕作变成耕作土壤，剖面分耕作层、犁底层、自然土层；种养结合（休耕、绿肥、轮作、广施农家肥）能保持土壤持续提供高效肥力的能力。
points: 自然土壤经过长期耕作培育就变成耕作土壤，剖面分耕作层、犁底层和自然土层。
耕作层又称表土层或熟土层：土质疏松、有机质比例高、颜色较暗；犁底层又称亚表土层：紧实、颜色较浅，能保肥保水；自然土层未经熟化，不利于作物生长。
只用不养，表层有机质降到 1.10 %；种养结合（休耕、种植绿肥、轮作、广施农家肥）回升到 1.61 %。

zh.q: 考核：把这块地育成一块肥沃的耕地
zh.concl: 肥沃的耕地要同时满足：质地壤土（母质与地貌合适）、表层有机质 ≥ 3 %（生物量够 + 积累条件好）、并且坚持种养结合。
points: 有机质要「有来源」：生物量得够，生物 0 % 时有机层直接消失。
还要「存得住」：冷湿比湿热更容易积累——温度高、雨多时有机质反而被分解掉。
质地看母质与地貌：壤质母质 + 山麓刚好是壤土；雨量只改黏粒占比，改不了质地名称。

en.q: How many layers can you make out in this soil sample from top to bottom?
en.concl: A soil profile is a vertical section from the surface downward, made of roughly horizontal layers with different features; among natural soils, forest soil profiles are the most complex, from top to bottom: organic, humus, eluvial, illuvial, parent material and bedrock layers.
points: Soil consists of four things: minerals, organic matter, water and air; in the field, look at color, texture and profile structure (textbook p.88).
A profile is a vertical section from the surface downward; the layers are roughly horizontal and result from substances being transformed, moved and accumulated.
Forest soil profiles are the most complex, with six layers from top to bottom: organic → humus → eluvial → illuvial → parent material → bedrock; organic matter decreases with depth.

en.q: How does soil texture change with different parent material?
en.concl: Parent material is the weathering product of rock and the material basis of soil development; it sets the mineral composition and nutrients of soil and affects its texture.
points: Parent material is the weathering product of rock and the material basis of soil development.
It sets the soil's mineral composition and nutrients and affects its texture: sandy parent material → gravelly soil / sand, clayey parent material → clay.
Rocks in the Sichuan Basin are purple and so is the soil; the dominant factor behind this is parent material.

en.q: Take away the vegetation. Would this still be soil?
en.concl: Organisms are the most basic and most active factor in soil development; organic remains supply organic matter, microbes turn it into humus, and biological cycling concentrates nutrients at the soil surface.
points: Organisms are the most basic and most active factor in soil development: without organisms, soil cannot form.
Organic remains supply soil with organic matter, which microbes turn into humus.
Biological cycling moves nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to the surface: at 0 % organisms the organic and humus layers vanish and organic matter is 0.

en.q: With the same parent material, do hot-wet and cold-dry climates grow the same soil?
en.concl: Heat and moisture set the pace of weathering and leaching: hot-wet regions form soil fast, with more clay, strong leaching and fast organic matter breakdown; cold-wet conditions favor organic matter build-up, dry-hot regions accumulate little.
points: The intensity and speed of rock weathering correlate positively with temperature and precipitation, so soil forms much faster in hot-wet regions than in cold-dry ones.
In hot-wet regions chemical weathering and leaching are strong and clay content is high; cold-wet conditions favor organic matter build-up, while dry, hot regions accumulate little.
Note: rainfall and temperature change only the clay share, not the texture name; texture is set by parent material and landform.

en.q: Are the soil particles on a hilltop as coarse as those on the plain at the foot of the hill?
en.concl: From hilltop to low-lying land, parent material particles go from coarse to fine, with gravelly soil, sand, loam and clay in turn; so hilltop soils are coarser and piedmont plains finer.
points: Landform affects soil development through heat and moisture and by sorting parent material particles.
From hilltop to low-lying land, parent material particles change from coarse to fine: gravelly soil → sand → loam → clay.
Loam has a balanced mix of sand, silt and clay, letting air and water through while holding water and nutrients: the ideal texture for farming.

en.q: How long does it take for 20 cm of soil to form?
en.concl: The longer soil develops, the thicker it gets and the more clearly its layers differentiate; under natural conditions 20 cm of arable soil generally takes 100–1,000 years to form.
points: The longer soil develops, the thicker it gets and the more clearly its layers differentiate.
Under natural conditions, forming 20 cm of arable soil generally takes 100–1,000 years.
So every centimeter in the column was "saved up": each layer of bedrock weathered away adds a layer of soil.

en.q: What does the profile look like after a plot has been farmed for a long time?
en.concl: Natural soil becomes cultivated soil after long farming, with a profile of plow layer, plow pan and natural soil layer; cropping with soil care (fallowing, green manure, rotation, plenty of farmyard manure) keeps soil able to supply high fertility over time.
points: Natural soil becomes cultivated soil after long farming, with a profile of plow layer, plow pan and natural soil layer.

The plow layer, also called topsoil or mature soil, is loose, high in organic matter and darker; the plow pan, also called the sub-topsoil, is compact and paler and holds nutrients and water; the natural soil layer is unimproved and poor for crops.
Use without care drops surface organic matter to 1.10 %; cropping with soil care (fallowing, green manure, crop rotation, plenty of farmyard manure) brings it back to 1.61 %.

en.q: Assessment: turn this plot into fertile farmland
en.concl: Fertile farmland needs all of these at once: loam texture (suitable parent material and landform), surface organic matter ≥ 3 % (enough biomass + good conditions for build-up), and sticking with cropping plus soil care.
points: Organic matter needs a "source": there must be enough biomass, and at 0 % organisms the organic layer simply disappears.
It also has to "be kept": cold-wet conditions accumulate it more easily than hot-wet ones, where heat and rain break it down instead.
Texture depends on parent material and landform: loamy parent material + foothill gives exactly loam; rainfall only changes the clay share, not the texture name.
